summary: Specifies how to find which Registration Data Access Protocol server is authoritative for a query, such as a domain name, IP address, or autonomous system number. It is an Internet Standard and obsoletes RFC 7484.

eli5.summary: A directory that tells you which office to ask about who owns a domain or address.

subtitle: How an RDAP client looks up which server to ask about a domain, an IP address or an AS number.

tldr.problem: The RDAP query documents say how to ask a registration data server a question, but not which server to ask for a given domain, IP address or AS number.
tldr.mechanism: IANA publishes JSON bootstrap registries for domains, IPv4, IPv6 and AS numbers. A client downloads and caches them, finds the longest match for its query and uses the base URL listed there.
tldr.outcome: A client can reach the authoritative RDAP server from data IANA already maintains. This Internet Standard obsoletes RFC 7484 with only minor clarifications.

facts.label: Registries
facts.value: Domain names, IPv4, IPv6, AS numbers

today: RFC 9224 is an Internet Standard (STD 95 in the header) published in March 2022. It obsoletes RFC 7484, with no substantive changes beyond minor clarifications, and has not itself been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem and the Approach
sections.content:
The Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) defines how to query and retrieve registration data from registries. Those documents (RFC 7480, RFC 7481, RFC 9082 and RFC 9083) do not say where to send a query. RFC 9224 fills that gap by specifying how to find the server that is authoritative for a requested scope.

The key observation is that Top-Level Domains, Autonomous System numbers and network blocks are already delegated by IANA to registries such as TLD registries and Regional Internet Registries. So the bootstrap data is best generated from data and processes IANA already maintains. IANA created new RDAP Bootstrap Service Registries in a JSON format, based on its existing registries. A client fetches them, extracts the data and matches its query against them to find the authoritative server and its base query URL.
sections.eli5: RDAP tells you how to ask a question, but not who to ask. This RFC adds a directory, kept by IANA, that says who to ask for each kind of thing.

sections.title: Structure of the Bootstrap Registries
sections.content:
Each registry is a JSON object with a version (this document defines "1.0"), a publication timestamp in Internet date/time format, an optional description and a services array. Each element of services is a two-element array: an Entry Array and a Service URL Array.

The Entry Array lists all entries that share the same set of base RDAP URLs, and the Service URL Array lists those URLs. Neither array is ordered. Base RDAP URLs MUST end with a trailing /, because query segments from RFC 9082 are appended to them. Where a list holds both HTTPS and HTTP URLs, clients SHOULD prefer the secure version and try it first.

JSON names MUST follow Section 6 of RFC 7480, and unrecognized JSON properties or values MUST be ignored. Internationalized domain labels MUST appear only in A-label form, and all domain labels MUST be lowercase.
sections.eli5: Each page of the directory has a list of names, and next to it a list of web addresses to ask about them. The addresses must end with a slash so the question can be tacked on the end.

sections.title: Finding the Server for a Domain Name
sections.content:
The domain registry lists domain labels attached to the root. The client finds the authoritative service by a label-wise longest match of the target domain against the entries, comparing label by label from right to left. If the longest match yields several entries, they are equivalent.

For a query about a.b.example.com, the com entry matches. The client picks one base URL from that entry's array and appends the segment from RFC 9082, giving https://registry.example.com/myrdap/domain/a.b.example.com in the RFC's example. If both com and example.com were listed, the longer example.com entry would win.

Matching is per label, not per character. With entries com and goodexample.com, a query for example.com matches only com. The root of the domain name space is written as an empty string "".
sections.eli5: To find the right office for a web name, you read it from the end, like finding a street by country first, then city. You pick the most specific entry that fits.

sections.title: Finding the Server for IP Addresses and AS Numbers
sections.content:
For IP address space the client does a longest match, done the same way as packet forwarding: addresses are converted to binary and compared up to the specified prefix length. This lets a covering prefix point to one server while a more specific prefix inside it points to another. IPv4 entries use CIDR notation (RFC 4632) and IPv6 entries use the text form of RFC 5952.

In the RFC's IPv4 example, a query for 192.0.2.1/25 matches both 192.0.0.0/8 and 192.0.2.0/24, and the latter wins as the longest match, giving https://example.org/ip/192.0.2.1/25. In the IPv6 example, a query for 2001:db8:1000::/48 picks 2001:db8:1000::/36 over 2001:db8::/34, and the client chooses the HTTPS URL. If the server does not answer, the client can try another URL from the array.

AS number entries are ranges written as two decimal numbers joined by a hyphen, such as 64512-65534, in increasing order. A single AS number is a range of two identical values, numbers use the asplain form and ranges MUST NOT overlap. A query for AS 65411 matches 64512-65534, giving https://example.net/rdaprir2/autnum/65411.
sections.eli5: For numbers, you look for the smallest box that still holds your number. A big box can send you to one office, while a smaller box inside it can send you to a different one.

sections.title: Client Behavior and Limits
sections.content:
Clients are expected to fetch the IANA registries and do the matching locally. They SHOULD NOT fetch a registry on every RDAP request. They SHOULD cache it and use signaling such as the HTTP Expires header to know when to refresh.

A registry may not contain the requested value. A newly allocated TLD, IP range or AS range is not guaranteed to have an entry yet, because its RDAP server may go live and be registered later. In that case there is no known RDAP server and the client SHOULD give the user an appropriate error message.

The method does not bootstrap everything. Entities (contacts, registrants, registrars) have no global name space, so this document does not say how to find their servers; the RFC suggests asking the server that returned the identifier, using a fully qualified URL, or using RFC 8521. Also not bootstrapped are search patterns without a matching terminating string, nameservers and help.
sections.eli5: You should copy the directory and keep it for a while instead of asking for it every time. Sometimes a new thing is not in the directory yet, and then you tell the user you could not find an office.

sections.title: Security and IANA Requirements
sections.content:
By providing a bootstrap method, the document helps ensure that users get RDAP data from an authoritative source rather than from rogue sources. The method has the same security properties as the RDAP protocols themselves, and the transport used to access the registries uses TLS.

IANA has created the registries as JSON objects. They MUST be accessible only through HTTPS, and the Content-Type returned MUST be application/json. The entries are generated from IANA's allocation registries plus the added RDAP server information, which differs from the normal IANA process, and the document changes none of the allocation policies. Because software will download these registries, IANA expects download demand to be unusually high and has put infrastructure in place to support the load.
sections.eli5: Because the directory comes from IANA over a protected connection, you can trust you are being sent to the real office and not a fake one.
